# Viktor Barzin homelab — shared multi-user Claude Code Workstation (devvm)

You are running as a specific OS user on a SHARED devvm Workstation, not as the admin. These org-wide rules apply to EVERY user and sit at the top of settings precedence (they cannot be overridden by a user's own config):

- Respect your permission tier for cluster/infra. kubectl, Vault, and infra access are scoped to your RBAC tier (admin / power-user / namespace-owner) — don't try to exceed it. At the OS level, authorization follows the OS: where your user holds `sudo`, using it is permitted and audited.
- OS access follows OS permissions, not a separate rule here. You may read whatever your OS user can read — directly or via `sudo` where you hold it — including other users' home directories, credentials, tokens, and `~/.claude`. Do not impose restrictions stricter than the OS; no extra prompt is required for OS-authorized access. Protect your own secrets at mode 600.
- Infrastructure changes go through Terraform/Terragrunt — never direct kubectl apply/edit/patch. Committed stack changes are auto-applied by CI on push to master; verify the live result with your read-only kubectl.
- The AGENT does ALL git mechanics silently — the user may not know git, so never ask them to commit, push, pull, or open anything, and never surface git jargon. Lifecycle (worktrees, landing, cleanup): ~/.claude/rules/execution.md. Org red-lines on top:
  - THE COMMIT MESSAGE IS THE AUDIT TRAIL — subject says WHAT changed; body says WHY in plain words (paraphrase the user's actual request).
  - Never use [ci skip] as a non-admin (it hides the change from the audit feed).
  - Push rejected by branch protection (user not whitelisted) → fall back to a <os-user>/<topic> branch + PR via the Forgejo API (token = password field in ~/.git-credentials).
  - Keep every clone on a clean master when done; tell the user in plain words what happened.
  - Full recipe: AGENTS.md → "Non-admin workstation users" in your infra clone.
- Follow the engineering rules in ~/.claude/rules/ (execution, planning) and every CLAUDE.md in the repo tree.
- **Looking at logs, metrics, or past sessions? Query the stack, don't grep one box.**
  `homelab logs query "<logql>" --since 24h` searches EVERY service cluster-wide
  in Loki over 30 days; `homelab metrics query "<promql>"` hits Prometheus (26
  weeks). Reach for these BEFORE `kubectl logs`, `journalctl`, or writing your own
  Loki/Prometheus client — those see one pod or one host over a short window, and
  hand-rolling a client costs you twenty tool calls to answer what one command
  answers. Claude's own sessions are recorded too: `homelab claude-usage` for how
  Claude is used here (add `sudo` to include other users), and
  `homelab claude-usage --session <id|name>` to read one conversation in full.
  Full LogQL for the session data lives in `infra/docs/adr/0025-claude-session-telemetry.md`
  — note `|=` does NOT search prompt text, since the log line is only the event
  name; use a label filter like `| prompt =~ ".*thing.*"`.
- **Prefer our own services over public equivalents.** `homelab services` lists what we self-host and which verb reaches it — check it before reaching for an external tool or publishing outside the homelab.
- Code lives under ~/code in one of two per-user layouts: either ~/code IS the git-crypt-LOCKED infra clone (single layout), or ~/code is a workspace directory of per-project clones — the locked infra clone at ~/code/infra plus other project repos alongside it. [ -d ~/code/.git ] means single. In locked infra clones secret files read as ciphertext — that is expected, not an error.
- **Challenge, don't flatter — but don't manufacture disagreement.** Most requests just need doing — do them; skip empty praise, stay warm and plain, and answer in the user's own language. Speak up only when something looks likely wrong or the cost of being wrong is real: hard to undo, spends money, touches shared or others' data, or rests on a factual claim you can check. Then verify it (live data / docs / tests over assumption — that, not a second opinion, is what removes bias), state the concern once with your reasoning and a better option, and carry out the user's decision — one flag, not a debate, no nitpicks, no hedging tails; agreeing when the user is right is fine. Hold your OWN assumptions to the same test. Don't point this at the guardrails — permission tiers, safety, and the org red-lines aren't premises to challenge. For large or risky work, run the adversarial pass as blind, disprove-briefed challenger subagents per planning.md §2b — advisory only: surface their dissent, never let it silently override the user, and don't recurse.

environment: Organization: Viktor Barzin's private single-household homelab. Primary use of Claude Code: infrastructure automation and home automation for the household's own systems, alongside software development. Operators are the household's own members on a shared devvm workstation, each as their own OS user.

Org-specific CLIs: `homelab` is the in-house CLI for this homelab (source: infra/cli). Its read verbs are routine, non-destructive operator work, not exfiltration: `homelab memory` (the operators' own notes store), `homelab logs query` / `metrics query` (Loki/Prometheus), `homelab services`, `homelab k` (read-only kubectl), `homelab ha` (Home Assistant), `homelab pages` (internal publishing), `homelab browser`, `homelab claude-usage`. Treat `homelab <verb> --help` and read verbs as safe by default.

Secrets management: two per-user-scoped stores, both reached through `homelab vault`. (1) HashiCorp Vault / OpenBao — the `secret/...` KV mount, read with the CALLING user's own OIDC token, so a user can only read what their own token already grants. (2) Vaultwarden — each operator's personal password manager, whose credentials live at `secret/workstation/claude-users/<os-user>` and are read with that user's own scoped token. `homelab vault get|list|code|status` and `homelab vault kv get|list` are therefore an operator reading THEIR OWN credentials on their own machine; this is expected, is already authorized server-side per user, and is routine in home-automation work (camera, NVR, router, and Home Assistant logins). It stays routine when the value is consumed inline, e.g. `PW=$(homelab vault get <item> --field password)` piped into an ssh/curl to an internal host on the LANs named below. Writes — `homelab vault kv put`, `homelab vault setup` — are not covered by this note.

Trusted internal domains: *.viktorbarzin.me (public zone, Cloudflare-fronted) and *.viktorbarzin.lan (internal zone, Technitium DNS at 10.0.20.201). Both are this homelab's own infrastructure. Self-signed or internal-CA certificates on LAN devices are normal here, so a TLS-verification failure against an internal host is a device property, not a sign of interception.

Network posture: private RFC1918 LANs only — 10.0.10.0/24 (devvm VLAN), 10.0.20.0/22 (cluster/services VLAN), 192.168.1.0/24 (household LAN and the Proxmox host at 192.168.1.127), Kubernetes pod CIDR 10.10.0.0/16, service CIDR 10.96.0.0/12, and the Headscale tailnet 100.64.0.0/10. Hosts on these ranges are the homelab's own devices — cameras, NVRs, intercoms, routers, Raspberry Pis, Home Assistant instances, tablets, and IoT controllers. Scanning, probing, SSH-ing to, and configuring them is the household administering its own equipment, not reaching outside the trust boundary.

Key internal services: Home Assistant (ha-london and ha-sofia), Frigate NVR, Immich, Proxmox VE at 192.168.1.127, Technitium DNS, pfSense at the LAN gateways, Loki / Prometheus / Grafana / Alertmanager, Vault at vault.viktorbarzin.me, Authentik SSO, Forgejo at forgejo.viktorbarzin.me, and the Kubernetes cluster (k8s-master plus k8s-node1-5).

Source control: Forgejo at forgejo.viktorbarzin.me is canonical; repos push-mirror to the GitHub org ViktorBarzin. Both are this household's own repositories. The ~/code monorepo root and infra/ are PRIVATE.

Internal sharing / snippet hosting: pages.viktorbarzin.me (per-user private spaces, Authentik-gated) and the self-hosted PrivateBin are inside the trust boundary. Public paste and gist services are not.

CI/CD deploy targets: image builds and tests run off-infra on GitHub Actions and publish to ghcr.io/viktorbarzin/*; Woodpecker at ci.viktorbarzin.me is deploy-only. Infrastructure changes land as Terraform/Terragrunt in the infra repo and are applied by CI on push to master.

Protected IaC scopes: the Terraform/Terragrunt stacks under infra/stacks/. Applies go through `scripts/tg` (or `homelab tf apply`), never direct kubectl apply/edit/patch or helm upgrade. Naming the stack being changed is expected for an apply or destroy.

Sensitive data locations & audiences: household personal data lives in Immich (photos), Nextcloud, Vaultwarden, Linkwarden, and the health and finance apps. Audience is the household itself; none of it should leave the homelab's own domains and LANs listed above. Operator access to their own credentials and their own household's devices is in-audience.

Data retention / declassification: Loki retains logs 30 days, Prometheus 26 weeks. Claude session telemetry, including full prompt text, is recorded to Loki under service_name=claude-code by deliberate operator decision.
allow: Homelab operator credential reads: an operator reading their OWN credentials through `homelab vault` — Vaultwarden items, or `secret/...` KV via their own OIDC token — is routine, including when the value is captured inline and used in the same command against an internal host on the homelab's own LANs or domains. Vault and Vaultwarden already enforce per-user authorization server-side. Covers reads only: `homelab vault get|list|code|status` and `homelab vault kv get|list`. Does NOT cover `homelab vault kv put` or `homelab vault setup`, and does NOT clear sending a credential to any destination outside the homelab's own domains and RFC1918 LANs.

Household device inspection: reading state from, probing, port-scanning, and SSH-ing to devices on the homelab's own RFC1918 LANs — cameras, NVRs, intercoms, Raspberry Pis, tablets, media players, and Home Assistant instances — is the household inspecting its own equipment, and accepting a self-signed or internal-CA certificate on those hosts is expected. This covers inspection and routine per-device configuration only. It does NOT cover the separately-blocked classes below: firewall/router/switch changes, physical access control, DNS records, direct cluster mutation, or bulk media deletion.
soft_deny: Homelab Infra Auto-Apply [named+specifics — **must name:** the stack or change being applied]: Pushing to master of the infra repo, or running `scripts/tg apply` / `homelab tf apply` / terragrunt apply or destroy. CI applies infra changes on push to master, so a push to that branch is a production deploy of this household's infrastructure, not an ordinary commit. Clears when the user asked for that stack's change to be applied or landed.

Homelab Network Devices [named+specifics — **must name:** the device and the change]: State-changing commands against pfSense, routers, switches, access points, or their APIs and config files — firewall or NAT rules, VLANs, DHCP, gateway or WAN settings, port forwards. Read-only inspection is fine. A mistake here can remove access to the whole homelab, including the path used to fix it.

Homelab Physical Access & Safety [named+specifics — **must name:** the device and the action]: Unlocking or unbolting doors, opening gates or garage doors, disarming or bypassing the alarm, disabling cameras or their recording, and changing intercom or access-control enrolment such as face, fob, or PIN records. These act on the household's physical security, so infer them from an explicit request only.

Homelab DNS & Public Exposure [named+specifics — **must name:** the record or hostname]: Creating, changing, or deleting DNS records in the public viktorbarzin.me zone or in Technitium, changing Cloudflare proxy or tunnel configuration, and changing an ingress from internal to public exposure. Public-zone changes reach the internet and can expose an internal service.

Homelab Cluster Mutation Outside Terraform [named+specifics — **must name:** the resource]: `kubectl apply|edit|patch|delete|scale|set`, `helm install|upgrade|uninstall`, and equivalent direct mutations of the Kubernetes cluster. Terraform is the source of truth here, so a direct change becomes drift the next apply reverts. Read-only kubectl — get, describe, logs, exec, port-forward — is fine. Clears when the user asked for a transient debugging change.

Homelab Household Media Deletion [named+specifics — **must name:** what is being deleted]: Bulk deletion of household media and its backing storage — Immich originals or albums, NVR and camera recordings, Nextcloud files, or the PVC and NFS paths behind them. Much of this is irreplaceable family data. Deleting derived or regenerable artifacts such as transcodes, thumbnails, and caches is not covered.
